summary:
The Cook Islands is self-governing in free association with New Zealand, which supplies nationality and passport rules; criminal and marriage law on the islands is made and applied locally.

Sex between men was decriminalised by the Crimes Amendment Bill, which Parliament passed on 14 April 2023 and which took effect on 1 June 2023. The provisions removed were sections 154 and 155 of the Crimes Act 1969, covering sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, with consent expressly excluded as a defence. Sources disagree on the maximum penalties: coverage from 2017 records up to seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while reporting on the repeal cites up to ten years for indecent acts between males. No source records a prosecution under these sections in living memory, and the note attached to the amending bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands.

The same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. It did not change the marriage law.

Marriage is defined by the Marriage Amendment Act 2000 as between a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing in the Cook Islands, and a marriage entered into abroad on that basis is not recognised locally.
tangentialFactors: The repeal concluded a reform process that had run since 2017, when a draft Crimes Bill written with New Zealand legal assistance would have removed sections 154 and 155; a select committee recommended deletion and the offences were struck from the draft, after which members reversed that decision and, in October 2020, deferred the bill's report by a further three months. Public submissions on the 2017 bill were taken by a parliamentary select committee in a country of roughly 21,000 people, and at least three lawyers were expected to address penalties and sentencing.
localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association is the country's LGBTI community organisation, and its submission was before the select committee examining the 2017 draft Crimes Bill. The offences struck from the draft at that stage were restored by members before the 2023 amendment finally removed them.

The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 continues to govern who may marry locally, so same-sex marriages cannot be entered into in the Cook Islands.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in the inventory addresses gender-marker or passport policy for trans travellers, gender-recognition procedures, healthcare access, facility use, hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection, or police practice in the Cook Islands. Nothing in the available sources documents a trans-specific prosecution, enforcement action or violent incident.

The maximum penalties recorded for the repealed sections 154 and 155 are inconsistent across sources: seven years and five years in the 2017 reporting, up to ten years in reporting on the repeal. The discrepancy is unresolved, and whether the offences were ever applied before living memory is not established either.
